title: Modern C++ Best Practices
content:
You are an expert in Modern C++ (C++17/20) development.

## Memory Management
- Use smart pointers (unique_ptr, shared_ptr) over raw pointers
- Avoid manual new/delete; use RAII throughout
- Use std::make_unique and std::make_shared
- Prefer value semantics where performance allows

## Concurrency
- Use std::thread or std::async for threading
- Use std::mutex, std::lock_guard for synchronization
- Prefer std::atomic over volatile for atomic operations
- Use std::promise/future for async result passing

## Performance
- Use constexpr for compile-time evaluation
- Use move semantics to avoid unnecessary copies
- Reserve container capacity when size is known
- Prefer algorithms over raw loops
- Use inline namespaces for ABI compatibility

## Code Quality
- Use the Core Guidelines Checker
- Prefer range-based for loops
- Use structured bindings for tuple/struct unpacking
- Mark overriding functions with override keyword
- Use noexcept for non-throwing functions

title: Modern C++20/23 Features & Best Practices
content:
You are an expert in Modern C++20/23 development.

## C++20 Key Features
- Concepts: template constraints with clear error messages
  template<std::integral T> or requires clause
- Ranges: pipeline-style data processing (views::filter | views::transform)
- Coroutines: co_await, co_yield, co_return for async code
- Three-way comparison (<=>): auto-generate all comparison operators with = default
- std::span: non-owning view over contiguous memory (replaces (ptr, len) pairs)
- constexpr virtual functions and try-catch in constexpr
- std::format: Python-style string formatting (safer than printf, faster than stringstream)
- Calendar and time zones: std::chrono extensions

## C++23 Notable Additions
- std::expected: error handling with either value or error (like Rust Result)
- std::mdspan: multidimensional array views
- std::flat_map / std::flat_set: sorted vector-based containers
- std::generator: coroutine-based lazy sequence generation
- if/constexpr with initializer
- std::print / std::println: direct printing to stdout

## Best Practices
- Use Concepts over SFINAE (simpler, better errors, faster compile)
- Use std::span for function parameters expecting contiguous sequences
- Use std::format/std::print over printf/iostreams in new code
- Use spaceship operator for types needing ordering
- Use Ranges to replace complex iterator loops
- Prefer std::optional for maybe-values, std::expected for fallible operations
- Use constexpr/consteval to move computation to compile time

## Performance Considerations
- Ranges views are lazy and composable (zero overhead unless materialized)
- std::format outperforms iostreams and sprintf
- Coroutines have allocation overhead; use for I/O, not tight loops
- Span: pass by value (sizeof span < sizeof string_view for some types)

title: CMake Build System Best Practices
content:
You are an expert in CMake build system design for C++ projects.

## Project Structure
- Use CMake 3.20+ for modern features
- Set minimum version: cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20...3.30)
- Use target-based design (target_sources, target_include_directories)
- Keep CMakeLists.txt per directory; source-tree visible in IDE
- Use add_library for all components (not add_executable for shared code)
- Use folder structure: src/, include/, tests/, third_party/

## Best Practices
- target_include_directories with PUBLIC/PRIVATE/INTERFACE
- target_link_libraries with PUBLIC/PRIVATE for transitive deps
- Use INTERFACE libraries for header-only components
- Use ALIAS targets for namespace consistency: MyLib::MyTarget
- Prefer FetchContent for dependency management (over ExternalProject)
- Use CTest for test registration and discovery
- Use CPack for packaging

## Presets & Toolchains
- Use CMakePresets.json for build configurations (debug, release, ci)
- Configure presets: generator, options, cache variables
- Build presets: configuration, jobs, targets
- Test presets: filter, parallel, output on failure
- Use toolchain files for cross-compilation

## Compiler & Build Optimization
- Set C++ standard per target: set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
- Use target properties for compile options, not global
- Enable PCH (Precompiled Headers) for large projects
- Use LTO/IPO for release builds
- Set BUILD_SHARED_LIBS for faster development linking
- Use ccache/compdb with CMake for caching

## Dependency Management
- Prefer FetchContent for third-party libraries
- Pin versions with GIT_TAG or URL_HASH
- Use find_package for system-installed libraries
- For package managers: vcpkg.json or Conanfile.py
- Export targets with install(EXPORT) for installed packages

title: Embedded C++ Development Best Practices
content:
You are an expert in embedded C++ development for constrained systems.

## Memory Constraints
- Avoid dynamic allocation (heap) in production code; use static allocation
- Use linker script sections for critical memory placement
- Prefer std::array over std::vector (fixed-size, no heap)
- Use placement new for pool-based allocation
- Know your memory layout: Flash, SRAM, external RAM, CCM
- Use constexpr for compile-time computation, reducing runtime memory

## Real-Time Constraints
- Avoid std::mutex in ISR context (use atomic or lock-free primitives)
- Use RAII for hardware resource management (GPIO, SPI, UART)
- Keep ISR functions minimal (set flag, wake task, exit)
- Use round-robin or priority-based scheduling
- Measure worst-case execution time (WCET) for critical paths
- Use volatile for memory-mapped registers and shared ISR variables

## Hardware Abstraction
- Template-based HAL for compile-time polymorphism (no vtable overhead)
- Static polymorphism with CRTP for device drivers
- Use constexpr/peripheral addresses as template parameters
- Separate hardware-specific code with compile-time conditions
- Use bit masks and bit-band regions for register manipulation

## C++ in Embedded
- Avoid exceptions (no unwind tables, RTTI overhead)
- Disable: -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics
- Use placement new for custom allocation strategies
- Prefer constexpr variables over macros for constants
- Use concepts for hardware trait constraints
- Use std::optional for register read results (without dynamic alloc)

## Testing & Debugging
- Unit test on host system with mocked hardware (GoogleTest)
- Use Semihosting or SEGGER RTT for debug output
- Use static analysis: Cppcheck, clang-tidy, PVS-Studio
- Analyze stack usage with -fstack-usage flag
- Profile with logic analyzer and oscilloscope for timing
- Use Coco/VectorCAST for MC/DC coverage in safety-critical systems

title: Modern C++ Smart Pointers and Memory Management
content: Modern C++ (C++11+) memory management: (1) std::unique_ptr - exclusive ownership, move-only, zero overhead over raw pointer, (2) std::shared_ptr - reference-counted ownership, control block overhead, (3) std::weak_ptr - break circular references with shared_ptr, (4) std::make_unique / std::make_shared - exception-safe allocation, (5) RAII - resource acquisition is initialization, destructors guarantee cleanup, (6) Rule of Five - if custom destructor/copy/move is needed, define all five. Avoid raw new/delete.

title: C++ Templates and Metaprogramming
content: C++ template metaprogramming: (1) Function templates and class templates with type/non-type parameters, (2) Template specialization - full and partial for custom behavior, (3) Variadic templates with parameter packs and fold expressions (C++17), (4) SFINAE with std::enable_if for compile-time dispatch, (5) constexpr and consteval for compile-time computation, (6) Concepts (C++20) for template constraints with readable error messages, (7) CRTP for static polymorphism. Prefer concepts over SFINAE.

title: C++ Concurrency and Parallelism
content: C++ concurrency (C++11+): (1) std::thread for OS threads, (2) std::async + std::future for task-based parallelism, (3) std::mutex, std::lock_guard, std::unique_lock for mutual exclusion, (4) std::atomic for lock-free operations on primitive types, (5) std::condition_variable for thread synchronization, (6) std::jthread (C++20) with automatic join, (7) Parallel algorithms (C++17) with execution policies (par, par_unseq, seq). Avoid deadlock with consistent lock ordering.

title: P.1: Express ideas directly in code 用代码直接表达意图
content: Express ideas directly in code rather than in comments. Good code is self-documenting. Use meaningful type names, variable names, and function names to express intent. Avoid comments that explain what the code does — instead, make the code clearer. If code is not clear enough, consider refactoring before adding comments. Compiler-enforced rules (types, const) are more reliable than human-enforced conventions.

title: P.2: Write in ISO Standard C++ 使用ISO标准C++编写
content: Write code conforming to the ISO C++ standard. Avoid compiler-specific extensions unless absolutely necessary for performance. Use '__restrict' and similar extensions only in carefully isolated sections. Prefer standard library facilities over platform-specific APIs. Set compiler flags to enforce standard conformance (e.g., -std=c++20 -pedantic-errors). This ensures portability across compilers and platforms.

title: P.3: Express intent 表达意图
content: State the intent of code clearly. Use the right types and constructs to express intent: use 'const' for values that should not change, 'final' for classes not designed for inheritance, and 'override' for virtual function overrides. Prefer 'enum class' over plain 'enum' for scoped enumerations. Use 'gsl::span' rather than pointer+size to express a range. Use structured bindings for destructuring. The type system and language features are your first line of documentation.

title: P.4: Ideally, a program should be statically type safe 理想情况下程序应静态类型安全
content: Strive for compile-time type safety. Avoid 'void*', unions, and casts where possible. Use 'variant' instead of unions, templates instead of 'void*', and 'gsl::not_null' for non-null pointers. Use 'std::optional' for nullable values, 'std::any' for type-erased values. If casts are necessary, prefer 'static_cast' (checked at compile time) over 'reinterpret_cast' or C-style casts. Enable 'gsl::narrow_cast' only when range is proven. Each cast is a potential type-safety violation.

title: P.5: Prefer compile-time checking to run-time checking 编译期检查优于运行时检查
content: Catch errors at compile time whenever possible. Use 'static_assert' for compile-time assertions. Use 'constexpr' and 'consteval' for compile-time evaluation. Prefer concepts (C++20) over SFINAE for template constraints — they provide better error messages. Use 'if constexpr' for compile-time conditional code. Compile-time checks are free at runtime and catch errors earlier in the development cycle.

title: P.6: What cannot be checked at compile time should be checkable at run time 运行时检查应尽可能
content: Design for runtime-checking of invariants that can't be verified at compile time. Use assertions ('assert', 'gsl::Expects', 'gsl::Ensures') to validate preconditions and postconditions. Consider contract programming with the GSL (Guidelines Support Library). Validate function inputs early (fail fast pattern). In debug builds, add extensive checking; in release builds, keep checks that prevent resource corruption. The cost of a runtime check is negligible compared to the cost of a silent data corruption.

title: P.7: Catch run-time errors early 尽早捕获运行时错误
content: Detect and report errors at the earliest possible point. Check function arguments at the top of the function. Validate return values immediately after calls. Use RAII to ensure resources are released even in error paths. Initialize all variables to sensible values — don't leave them uninitialized. Consider using 'gsl::span' with bounds checking in debug builds. Early detection localizes bugs and makes debugging significantly easier.

title: P.8: Don't leak any resources 不泄漏任何资源
content: All acquired resources must be released. Use RAII wrappers: 'std::unique_ptr' for exclusive ownership, 'std::shared_ptr' for shared ownership, 'std::vector' for dynamic arrays. Ownership should be clear and explicit — prefer passing by value or reference over raw pointers. 'std::string', 'std::vector' manage their own memory. If you write 'new'/'delete' or 'malloc'/'free' directly, you're likely doing something wrong. Never use 'malloc'/'free' in C++ code. Use 'gsl::owner' to document ownership when raw pointers are unavoidable.

title: P.9: Don't waste time or space 不浪费时间和空间
content: Be mindful of performance but don't optimize prematurely. Use move semantics to avoid copies: 'std::move' for lvalues, 'std::forward' for perfect forwarding. Use 'reserve' on containers when size is known. Prefer compact data structures: 'std::array' over 'std::vector' for fixed-size, small vectors on stack. Access memory predictably (linear access patterns). Avoid allocating in hot paths. However, correctness and clarity take priority over micro-optimization. Profile before optimizing.

title: P.10: Prefer immutable data to mutable data 不可变数据优先于可变数据
content: Use 'const' for values that don't change after initialization. Prefer 'constexpr' for compile-time constants. Make member functions 'const' when they don't modify the object. Use 'std::string_view' for read-only string parameters. Immutable data is easier to reason about, thread-safe by default, and enables compiler optimizations. If a value must change, keep the scope of mutation as small as possible.

title: P.11: Encapsulate messy constructs 封装混乱的结构
content: Hide complex, low-level, or dangerous code behind clean abstractions. Encapsulate casts in well-tested functions. Wrap platform-specific code in abstraction layers. Use interface classes to hide implementation details. Don't let messy constructs leak into high-level code — they spread confusion. A well-designed wrapper limits the blast radius of bugs and simplifies maintenance.

title: P.12: Use supporting tools as appropriate 适当使用工具
content: Use static analyzers (Clang-Tidy, PVS-Studio, CodeQL) to catch issues automatically. Run sanitizers in debug builds: AddressSanitizer (ASan), UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan), ThreadSanitizer (TSan), MemorySanitizer (MSan). Use valgrind for deeper analysis. Enable all warnings and treat them as errors (-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror). Use formatters (clang-format) and linters as pre-commit hooks. CI pipelines must include static analysis — it's the cheapest bug-fix you'll ever get.

title: P.13: Use support libraries as appropriate 适当使用支持库
content: Use well-established libraries rather than reinventing wheels. Use the C++ Standard Library extensively — it's part of the language. Consider GSL (Guidelines Support Library) for span, not_null, and narrow_cast. Use Boost for functionality not yet in the standard (filesystem before C++17, asio for networking). Use {fmt} library for type-safe formatting (standardized in C++20 as std::format). Prefer libraries with wide adoption, active maintenance, and good documentation.

title: F.1: Package operations as functions 将操作封装为函数
content: A function should perform a single logical operation. Give it a descriptive name. Keep functions short — if a function exceeds 20-30 lines, consider splitting it. A function should be understandable at a glance. If you need to read the implementation to know what it does, either the name is wrong or the function does too much. Good functions enable higher-level reasoning about code.

title: F.2: A function should perform a single logical operation 函数应执行单一逻辑操作
content: A function should do one thing and do it well. If a function has multiple responsibilities, it becomes harder to name, test, and reuse. Signs of multiple responsibilities: the function has 'and' in its description, or you need multiple paragraphs to explain it. Extract sub-operations into named helper functions. This improves readability and enables code reuse. Testing is simpler when each function has a single clearly defined behavior.

title: F.3: Keep functions short and simple 保持函数简短
content: Short functions are easier to understand and test. Aim for functions that fit on a screen (~20-40 lines). Extract complex conditions into named boolean functions. Extract repeated patterns into helper functions. Deeply nested if/switch statements indicate the function should be split. However, don't split a function arbitrarily — each resulting function should represent a meaningful concept. A function that's 5 lines but requires 50 lines of comments is worse than a well-structured 30-line function.

title: F.4: If a function may have to be evaluated at compile time, declare it constexpr 可编译期计算的函数声明为constexpr
content: Use 'constexpr' for functions that can potentially be evaluated at compile time. C++20 allows constexpr virtual functions, try/catch, and dynamic allocations. Constexpr functions enable compile-time computation, template metaprogramming, and better optimization. They also serve as documentation: a constexpr function can be used in static_assert and template arguments. When in doubt, make a function constexpr — it's a non-binding hint to the compiler.

title: F.5: If a function is very small and time-critical, declare it inline 小且时间敏感的函数声明为inline
content: Use 'inline' for very small, frequently-called functions (accessors, simple predicates). Modern compilers make inlining decisions automatically based on optimization flags. inline is now primarily a linkage directive (to avoid ODR violations in header files) rather than an optimization hint. Prefer defining trivial functions in class definitions (implicitly inline). For larger functions, trust the compiler's inlining heuristics with appropriate optimization flags (-O2/-O3).

title: F.6: If your function may not throw, declare it noexcept 不抛异常的函数声明为noexcept
content: Use 'noexcept' for functions that are guaranteed not to throw exceptions. Move operations, swap, and destructors should be noexcept. This enables compiler optimizations and enables move semantics (containers prefer noexcept move constructors). A noexcept function gives callers confidence — they don't need try/catch. Be careful: a noexcept function that throws will call std::terminate. Only mark functions noexcept if you're certain they won't throw.

title: F.8: Prefer pure functions 优先纯函数
content: A pure function's return value depends only on its arguments (not on global state), and it has no side effects. Pure functions are easier to: (1) reason about — same input always same output, (2) test — no setup/mocking needed, (3) parallelize — no shared state, (4) memoize — caching is trivial. Minimize mutation of function arguments. Avoid modifying global or static variables. In C++, const member functions and pass-by-value encourage pure function style.

title: F.9: Unused parameters should be unnamed 未使用的参数应无名
content: Leave unused function parameters unnamed (or comment them out) to suppress compiler warnings. Example: 'void foo(int /*unused*/)' or 'void foo(int)'. This clearly communicates intent to readers and static analyzers. If the parameter might be used conditionally (e.g., in debug builds), use a cast: '(void)param;'. Consider whether an unused parameter indicates a design issue before removing its name.

title: I.1: Make interfaces explicit 使接口显式化
content: Design interfaces that are clear about what they expect and what they provide. Prefer pass-by-value or pass-by-reference over pass-by-pointer (null not expected). Use 'gsl::not_null<T>' for parameters that must not be null. Document preconditions and postconditions. Use 'explicit' for single-argument constructors. Avoid 'const_cast', 'static_cast' on downcasts, and C-style casts — they hide interface contracts. Explicit interfaces are caught by the compiler; implicit ones are caught in code review (or worse, production).

title: I.2: Avoid non-const global variables 避免非const全局变量
content: Non-const global variables are: (1) a hidden dependency — any function might modify them, (2) a threading hazard — concurrent access needs synchronization, (3) a testing nightmare — tests can't run in isolation. Alternatives: pass parameters explicitly, use singletons (with caution), encapsulate in a class (dependency injection). If global state is unavoidable, make it const, thread-safe, and document its purpose. Consider using a context object passed through the call chain.

title: I.3: Avoid singletons 避免单例模式
content: Singletons introduce global state and hidden dependencies. They make testing difficult, prevent parallelization, and create implicit coupling. Alternatives: dependency injection, factory functions, passing objects explicitly. If you must use a singleton, ensure it's: (1) const (immutable after initialization), or (2) thread-safe with proper synchronization, and (3) has a well-defined lifetime. Scott Meyers' 'Magic Static' (static local variable) is thread-safe in C++11+.

title: I.4: Make interfaces precisely and strongly typed 精确且强类型的接口
content: Use the type system to express interface contracts. Bad: 'double get_value(int kind, const std::string& name, int options);' Better: 'class WidgetId { ... }; class WidgetOptions { ... }; Widget get_widget(WidgetId id);' Use dedicated types for parameters (minutes, not int). Use std::chrono for time. Strong types prevent parameter ordering bugs, make interfaces self-documenting, and enable compiler error checking. The cost of defining a small type is minimal.
